service_requirements.title: Trade-offs between price, wait, and comfort

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who uses ride-hailing and how often, then moves into the trip context and modal alternatives. It then explores the purchase journey — what triggers a ride, how apps are compared, and what drives the final choice — along with spend. Next, it captures service requirements and trade-offs, including safety, green options, and value. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, and switching risk, allowing segmentation by price sensitivity and usage intensity.
metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each ride-hailing app user belongs to, based on trip frequency, price sensitivity, modal choice, and feature priorities.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Price sensitivity combined with usage intensity — because in a mature, competitive market with low brand loyalty, the key axis separating buyers is how they trade off cost against convenience and comfort, and how often they actually use the service.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Occasionals Users
segments.description: Use ride-hailing rarely, mostly for airport trips or late-night outings when no other option works. They compare prices across apps, avoid surge pricing, and often choose public transit or driving if cheaper.
segments.hypothesis: They will report low trip frequency, high price sensitivity, and will prioritize cost over wait time or comfort.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Use ride-hailing regularly for commuting and errands, valuing reliability and short wait times over price. They are willing to pay moderate premiums to avoid being late, but still compare apps for the best balance.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high trip frequency, moderate price sensitivity, and will prioritize wait time and driver reliability over cost.

segments.name: Premium Comfort Buyers
segments.description: Frequent users who choose premium ride options for comfort, vehicle quality, and professional drivers. They are the least price-sensitive and will pay for a consistently high-quality experience.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high trip frequency, low price sensitivity, and will prioritize vehicle quality and driver professionalism over cost.

segments.name: Safety & Eco-Conscious Riders
segments.description: Moderate-frequency users who actively choose ride-hailing for safety (especially at night) and prefer green vehicle options. They are willing to pay more for safety features and EVs, and are sensitive to driver identity verification.
segments.hypothesis: They will report moderate trip frequency, medium price sensitivity, and will prioritize safety features and green options over cost or speed.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question that best settles a tie is bb6 ("When choosing between ride-hailing apps, which one matters most to you?") because it directly asks the respondent to prioritize the single most important attribute (price, wait, safety, or comfort), which is the core differentiator among the four segments.
notes: Frequency questions (cp4, bb7) are used as strong signals but not decisive alone because they are correlated with multiple segments.
Some options like 'Going out at night' are scored only weakly for safety segment because they are common across segments.
The scoring model ensures each segment has at least one 3-point option and multiple 2-point options.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
